sampling_method: CLIP is a two-column ICML-style paper, so reading order has to say how the columns are resolved. The order used is: page order; within a page, a float that spans both columns is read at its vertical position (top-of-page floats before both columns), and otherwise the left column top-to-bottom then the right column top-to-bottom, with a single-column float read where it sits in its own column. That order was checked against page images for pages 8, 21, 40 and 44 -- page 8 reads as left-column prose, then Figure 5 at the top of the right column, then the prose below it; page 21 reads as Table 3 (top left), Table 4 (top right), Table 5 (full width), then Section 7.1 left then right; page 44 reads as Appendix B and Appendix C down the left column, then Table 12 and Appendix D down the right -- and follows the block order of the page-text rendering elsewhere. Within a table, cells are indexed row-major and left-to-right across that row's own-result columns only; within a figure that prints per-item values, cells are indexed in the figure's drawn order (for the horizontal bar charts, top bar first: Figure 5 was verified against the page image and runs StanfordCars +28.9 at the top down to EuroSAT -37.1 at the bottom, which is the reverse of the order the text dump emits its labels in). That assigns every own-result cell in frame_locations a contiguous 1-based index, giving a population of 1..2441. Ownership is the decision this paper turns on, and it is settled per cell rather than per row. CLIP re-evaluates a large amount of prior work itself, and Appendices A.2 and A.3 are the evidence: A.2 lists the released checkpoints the authors downloaded (nine EfficientNets plus ten noisy-student variants, six Instagram ResNeXts, twelve BiT-S/BiT-M, four ImageNet-21k ViTs, seven SimCLRv2, two BYOL, two MoCo, VirTex, three original ResNets) and A.3 gives the logistic regression they fitted on each one's penultimate features. Every one of Table 10's 1782 cells is therefore an own result -- the authors' own rerun of a prior model -- and no citation appears anywhere in that table's body. The same reading makes Table 14's 'ES Best' row own (it 'reports the best performance across the 56 non-CLIP models in our evaluation suite', and 98.9 / 58.6 / 59.0 are traceable to Table 10's NS L2-475 and Instagram FixRes rows; the superscripts h and i name which model reached the score, not where the number came from), and makes Table 15's linear 'NS ENet-L2' row own despite its citation superscript, because the caption says outright that 'linear CLIP and linear NS ENet-L2 are trained and evaluated on a single frame subsampled version of each dataset'. Table 3, Table 4 and Table 5's 'Linear Probe Instagram' rows are own for the same reason, and the 'FairFace Model' rows in Tables 3 and 4 are read as own too: Section 7.1 frames the comparison as 'the classification tests we ran', and footnote 7 records that the FairFace model had to be reconciled to a binary White / Non-White race split that its own paper does not report. That last one is the frame's least certain call; it is worth 6 of 2441 cells. In the other direction, ownership is refused wherever a citation carries the number: Table 1's 'Visual N-Grams' row, Table 13's nine non-CLIP rows (the caption states 'For all other models, best results from the paper are reported'), Table 14's SOTA / JOINT / CBoW rows, Table 15's five finetune and zero-shot baseline rows, Table 16's two Taori-suite rows, Table 17's four cited geolocalization systems, Figure 13's 'ImageNet ResNet101' row, and the Introduction's 11.5% / 88.4% / 50% / 5%. Deltas: a delta counts only where no absolute is printed beside it. That excludes Table 12's two Delta columns (each the difference of the two absolutes printed immediately to its left), Figure 13's Delta Score row (each delta printed directly under the two absolutes it is computed from), and the 9.2% in 'increases its ImageNet accuracy by 9.2% to 85.4% overall'. It includes, as printed reported numbers with no absolute beside them, all 27 of Figure 5's bars, all 27 of Figure 11's bars, all 16 of Figure 14's bars, and the prose deltas at 1.3%, 3.5%, almost 5%, 14.5%, 7.7%, almost 5% (page 9), 2.6%, 5%, 14.7%, 4.7/3.8/2.8/1.9%, 5%, 2.3%, 0.7 points and 10 points. Where the same measurement is restated at a different location it is counted again, following the convention that each printed instance at a new location is its own printed number; where a figure's caption restates a value already printed in that same figure's body (Figure 7's 184, Figure 14's 9.2%, Figure 4's 5 points and 4x, Figure 2's 3x and 4x) it is not counted twice, since caption and plot are one location. Excluded as not result cells, consistently throughout: ranges and bounds ('by over 20%', '10% to 25%', '97-100%', 'between 1 and 2 points', 'within 1%', 'up to +/-20%', the 95th-percentile interval 0.93-1.79 and every bracketed confidence interval); tallies of how many datasets a model wins on, which are counts rather than measurements -- this removes 'wins on 16 of the 27 datasets', '21 of the 27 datasets', '9 datasets have no detected overlap', '5 of the 7 datasets' and, in a table, Table 12's Dataset 'Wins' row; multipliers written as English words rather than digits ('twice the compute', 'three times slower', 'more than doubles the accuracy'), on the same footing as bit's exclusion of 'around half'; dataset statistics, which here include the 400M pair count, all per-dataset class and split sizes in Table 9, and the data-overlap rates (median 2.2%, average 3.2%, Country211's 21.5%, Birdsnap's 12.1%) -- a contamination rate is a property of the data, the same call that excluded bit's near-duplicate counts, while the accuracy shifts those overlaps cause (0.6%, 0.2%, 20%) are counted; hyperparameters and training cost, including the RN50x64's '18 days to train on 592 V100 GPUs' and the '405 years' illustration; and Figure 21's 36 'correct rank' / 'correct probability' pairs, which report the model's output on one randomly chosen image each in an explicitly qualitative figure rather than a measured outcome on a dataset (a reviewer who disagrees would add 72 cells there). Figures 1, 3, 6, 9, 10, 12, 15, 16, 18, 19, 20 and 22 print only axis-tick calibration, legends and names and count 0; the unusual thing about this paper is how many of its figures do print values, and Figures 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 11, 13, 14 and 17 together contribute 109 cells. The Abstract contributes 0: it states no numeric performance value of its own. random.seed(20260810); random.sample(range(1, 2442), 15) drew {3, 19, 200, 222, 392, 449, 1109, 1323, 1454, 1573, 1711, 1725, 1948, 2355, 2436}; each label below records its draw as frame_index. Nine of the fifteen land in Table 10 (page 40), two in Table 5 (page 21), one in Table 12 (page 44), one in Figure 5 (page 8) and two in prose (pages 4 and 47). Page images were rendered for exactly four pages of the same unchanged PDF -- 8, 21, 40 and 44 -- and every row-and-column attribution below was checked against them; page 21 was also what settled Table 5's cell count, since only the page image shows that two of its three combined rows leave the Average cell blank (70 printed cells, not 72). The two prose draws are sequential and needed no image.

labels.notes: 'CLIP improves over the prior state of the art, a S3D model trained on automatically extracted captions from 100 million instructional videos, by 10 points.' A delta, counted because no absolute is printed beside it -- both absolutes are in Table 15 on page 46, a different location. Own: the improvement is CLIP's own zero-shot RareAct result over the quoted HT100M S3D baseline. One thing a reviewer should note: the sentence does not say which of RareAct's two metrics it means, and Table 15 reports both -- the mWSAP delta is exactly 44.8 - 34.8 = 10.0 and the mWAP delta is 40.7 - 30.5 = 10.2, so '10 points' matches mWSAP exactly and rounds mWAP. The metric is recorded as the sentence prints it rather than resolved to one of the two.
